headings.title: Introduction to Blood Analysis in Medical Surgical Nursing
headings.content: Blood analysis serves as a window into the internal environment of your patient. In medical-surgical nursing, you look at these laboratory numbers constantly to catch small physiological shifts before they turn into major clinical crises. Every blood draw tells a story about oxygen transport, fluid balance, infection, or organ function. Learning to read these reports accurately helps you plan safer care, question suspect orders, and report meaningful changes to the medical team.

headings.title: Components of Blood and Normal Laboratory Values
headings.content:
Blood is composed of formed elements suspended in plasma. Plasma makes up about 55% of total blood volume, acting as the fluid transport medium for nutrients, hormones, and waste products. The remaining 45% consists of cellular components: erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes.

- **Erythrocytes (Red Blood Cells)**: Carry oxygen from the lungs to the tissues using hemoglobin. Normal adult range is roughly 4.2 to 5.4 million per microliter.
- **Leukocytes (White Blood Cells)**: Protect the body against infection and foreign invaders. Normal range is typically 4,500 to 11,000 per microliter.
- **Thrombocytes (Platelets)**: Essential cellular fragments that promote blood clotting and plug vascular leaks. Normal range is 150,000 to 450,000 per microliter.

headings.title: Complete Blood Count (CBC) and Differential Interpretation
headings.content:
A complete blood count gives you a detailed breakdown of cellular elements. When looking at hemoglobin and hematocrit, you evaluate the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. Low hemoglobin points toward anemia or acute hemorrhage, while an elevated count may indicate dehydration or chronic hypoxia.

The differential looks closer at white blood cell types. Neutrophils rise sharply during acute bacterial infections. Lymphocytes increase in viral infections. Eosinophils often climb during allergic reactions or parasitic invasions. Analyzing these shifts gives you sharp clues about the root cause of systemic inflammation.

headings.title: Coagulation Studies: PT, PTT, INR, and Platelet Function
headings.content:
Hemostasis requires a delicate balance between clotting and bleeding. Coagulation studies help you monitor this balance, especially when patients take anticoagulant medications.

| Test | What it Monitors | Common Therapeutic Target |
|---|---|---|
| Prothrombin Time (PT) / INR | Extrinsic pathway; monitored during Warfarin therapy | INR 2.0 to 3.0 for standard conditions |
| Partial Thromboplastin Time (PTT) | Intrinsic pathway; monitored during Heparin therapy | 1.5 to 2.5 times normal baseline |
| Platelet Count | Cellular clotting capability | Above 50,000 to prevent spontaneous bleeding |

A common clinical mistake is ignoring baseline values before starting a continuous infusion. Always check your baseline PTT before hanging a heparin drip so you can calculate subsequent adjustments safely.

headings.title: Blood Chemistry Panels and Electrolyte Balance
headings.content: Electrolytes govern electrical impulses, fluid distribution, and acid-base balance across cell membranes. Sodium governs serum osmolality and central nervous system function. Potassium is critical for cardiac rhythm; even small shifts outside the normal range can trigger lethal dysrhythmias. Kidney function markers like blood urea nitrogen and creatinine reveal how well the body filters metabolic waste. When creatinine climbs steadily, filtration is failing, signaling a potential acute kidney injury.

headings.title: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) Analysis and Acid-Base Balance
headings.content: Arterial blood gases measure how well the lungs oxygenate blood and how well the lungs and kidneys manage pH balance. Normal blood pH ranges tightly from 7.35 to 7.45. When pH falls below 7.35, the patient is in acidemia. When it rises above 7.45, alkalemia is present. Respiratory disorders alter carbon dioxide levels, while metabolic disorders shift bicarbonate levels. Systematic interpretation requires evaluating pH, carbon dioxide, and bicarbonate step by step to identify the primary imbalance and any compensatory responses.

headings.title: Nursing Responsibilities in Specimen Collection and Handling
headings.content: Accurate lab results depend entirely on proper specimen collection. Meticulous patient identification prevents dangerous lab mix-ups. When drawing blood from an extremity with an intravenous line, you must avoid drawing above the infusion site to prevent fluid contamination of the sample. For arterial blood gases, performing an Allen test ensures collateral circulation to the hand before puncturing the radial artery. Once collected, tubes must be inverted gently as required, labeled at the bedside, and transported promptly to avoid sample hemolysis.

headings.title: Clinical Implications of Abnormal Results and Patient Management
headings.content: Laboratory values never exist in a vacuum; you must always interpret them alongside your physical assessment. A critical panic value requires immediate notification of the provider and urgent bedside evaluation. If a patient's potassium level hits 6.8 mEq/L, you prepare for emergency interventions like administering intravenous insulin and glucose to shift potassium back into the cells. Documenting your clinical actions and communicating trends clearly ensures safe, continuous nursing care across shifts.
